extracted.intended_audience: foreign lecturers, travelers, and general readers interested in Japanese audiences, etiquette, and garden aesthetics
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and cultural guidance for foreigners who address Japanese audiences (public lectures, classes, and civic gatherings), plus criteria for appreciating/arranging Japanese gardens and floral art. Covers audience etiquette, lecture format, social status of teachers, and garden aesthetics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extraordinary patience in listening / audience endurance
rubrics_metrics.description: Japanese audiences show extraordinary patience in listening: whatever the subject, whoever the speaker, and whether the treatment is interesting or dull or even totally unintelligible, the listeners seem to feel the obligation to maintain the same attitude of attention to the very end of the discourse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speakers must be prepared for long periods of attention and endurance; expect that few will leave before the ceremonially proper time. Examples: large audiences listening two to three hours (Osaka, Kyoto); classes sustaining series of thirty or twenty lectures with high constancy of attendance; cultural tendency means entertainment-only talks are poorly appreciated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lecture format — double lecture and interpreter alternation
rubrics_metrics.description: Customary lecture structure: double lecture (e.g., fifty minutes' talk, ten minutes' tea, fifty minutes more). When interpretation is needed the address is often divided into five or six parts (~10 minutes each) with lecturer and interpreter alternating in regular order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow for greatly stretched engagement time when interpretation is used (often less than half the time is English; remainder for Japanese paraphrase). Some interpreters may render the entire lecture fluently and elegantly at the close; plan pacing and content accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ceremonial politeness and lecture protocol
rubrics_metrics.description: A formal ceremonial procedure is observed in lectures: a select party meets the lecturer beforehand; upon entry the entire audience rises and remains standing until the speaker has mounted the platform and bowed; at the close the audience rises and bows again and is expected to remain standing until the teacher has left the hall.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foreign speakers should respect and follow these protocols—do not expect the audience to begin dispersing early. Organisers commonly announce any special arrangements (e.g., to keep the teacher for further exercises). Violations may be seen as impolite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal and genuinely-held politeness
rubrics_metrics.description: Politeness in Japanese intercourse is formal and elaborate and carries a fair degree of genuineness; disregard of these observances is regarded as shocking rather than merely quaint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat Japanese politeness as mere ceremony; failure to comply with native forms (e.g., disrespect toward a servant) can be gravely offensive. Note that modern changes (costume, customs) complicate some native forms (e.g., kimono etiquette vs. standing courtesies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect for the teacher (Sensei) and teacher's social rank
rubrics_metrics.description: A proper respect for the teacher requires pupils to receive and salute him while standing. Teachers (Professors, President of Teacher's Association) hold high official rank and social standing; the truly successful teacher may wield influence comparable to major historical teachers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To gain influence in Japan one must win the claim to be a 'teacher' in its highest meaning; the title implies esteem and authority. Foreigners addressing audiences who are regarded as pupils should be conscious of this role and its responsibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Students' earnestness, exactingness, and readiness to judge
rubrics_metrics.description: Student audiences are eager, earnest, and often severe/extreme in judging the ability and moral character of their teachers; they may mobilise (e.g., strikes) to demand a teacher's removal if judged incompetent or unsafe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speakers/teachers should not assume passivity; be prepared for critical assessment and high expectations. Rapid student enthusiasm can lead to overcommitment to lecture-hours; organisers and teachers should balance volume with sound scholarship.

rubrics_metrics.name: High national valuation of education
rubrics_metrics.description: Japanese society at large prizes education highly: education is officially emphasised (Minister of Education ranks with other ministers), professors have court rank, graduates in trade schools are required to know English, and illiteracy proportions are low.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When addressing Japanese audiences assume a deep respect for instruction and for authoritative, morally-concerned discourse. This cultural valuation conditions receptivity to educational and ethical talks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for moral and ethical topics (post-war moral seriousness)
rubrics_metrics.description: There was strong nationwide demand for discussion of moral, educational, economic, and political problems as affected by moral conditions and principles; lectures on practical moral instruction (e.g., 'Doctrine of the Virtues as applied to Modern Business') were eagerly welcomed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Addresses that frame national prosperity, education, business, or service in moral/ethical terms resonate strongly; speakers should consider moral framing and the moral implications of topics, especially in times of national introspection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Japanese garden art core characteristics (Baron Kuki's three features)
rubrics_metrics.description: According to Baron Kuki: (1) mildness and pure simplicity (sober colouring, moderation), (2) exquisite lightness or delicacy (charming workmanship), and (3) idealism in representation (not realistic; abstraction of essential aspects).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these three features as primary evaluative criteria when judging Japanese gardens or other native art: prefer moderation over extravagance, fine craftsmanship, and expressive idealism rather than photographic realism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Garden composition: nature 'combed and trimmed' — controlled artificiality
rubrics_metrics.description: The Japanese art of gardening is not pure wild nature but 'nature excessively combed and trimmed' — every tree and shrub is cultivated and pruned with attention to details; decayed or superfluous elements are removed or selected to contribute artistically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate gardens by the intentionality of their control: pruning, cleaning of worn stones, selection of worm-eaten wood for fantasy patterns, and deliberate arrangement of decayed elements to express sentiment. Maintenance and careful placement are essential to the aesthetic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberate use and presentation of decay and miniature realism
rubrics_metrics.description: Worn rocks, worm-eaten woods, bare trunks, broken stumps, and other signs of decay have an important place, but must be carefully placed, kept scrupulously clean, and arranged so their shapes are defined by backgrounds of foliage or sky; gardens commonly present miniature mountains, rivers, lakes, waterfalls, forest, and sea-coast in small space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appreciation requires attention to scale and to the artist's abstraction: the garden aims to 'abstract the essential aspect of objects' within a small area. Small-scale realism and carefully curated decay are positive aesthetic devices, not defects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sympathetic aesthetic attitude required to appreciate gardens
rubrics_metrics.description: For aesthetic appreciation of the Japanese garden in its pure native form, a sympathetic share in the characteristic sentimental attitude toward nature is indispensable; without it one may judge the garden as artificially petty or excessively detailed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics lacking this sympathetic temperament should temper judgments by recognising the social and educational value of the garden (quiet, refining enjoyment of nature) and the non-vulgar intentions behind the style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Floral art and indoor arrangement criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Inside-floral arrangements should consider the character and uses of the room, the season, the nature of the festival or ceremonial occasion, the other art-objects and furniture of the same and adjoining rooms, and the scenery of the garden and the remoter landscape upon which the room opens. Some suggest contrast in style with the adjoining garden.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose plant materials (notably pine, bamboo, willow, and flowering trees) and arrangement style to suit room function, seasonality, festival meaning, and visual relation to the garden; employ flowerless trees effectively and respect cultural calendar traditions (e.g., plum blossoms herald spring).
